title: Piece activity: fix the worst piece first
outcomes: Lists how many squares each of his pieces reaches and names the worst-placed one before a quiet move
Prefers the move that most improves that piece over a pawn push, after checking the new square is safe
Notices when a loose enemy piece makes the activity question moot

steps.text:
In **Active and passive pieces** you counted the squares a piece reaches. Now use the count to choose a move. In a quiet position, list your pieces, find the **worst-placed** one (fewest squares, least to do), and ask which move gives it the most. A pawn push needs its own reason; a piece improvement usually has one built in.
**Rule of thumb:** improve the worst piece before pushing pawns.

steps.caption: Black to move. The bishop on e6 reaches five squares and the knight on f4 attacks it.

line.say: The bishop steps out of the knight's attack to f5, where it attacks nine such squares.
White makes a quiet rook move.
Black castles; the bishop is already better placed.

claims.statement: The bishop on e6 attacks 5 squares not held by Black.
Bf5 is within 30 centipawns of the engine's first choice (castling).

steps.text:
Three checks before you improve a piece.
**Is the new square safe?** More squares do not help if the piece can be taken.
**Is something loose or attacked?** Deal with that first.
**Is the count telling the truth?** Squares are a **rule of thumb**: an advanced piece can have fewer useful squares than a retreated one, and the count ignores what the squares are worth.

steps.title: Same bishop, one change
steps.prompt: In the first position Black's bishop move is right. In each of the next two, one thing has changed. Predict what it does to the plan, then check.
Before you counted squares in the last position: which of your pieces did you expect to be the worst placed? Did the count agree, or did a loose piece change the question?
